subject: math
cluster: Understand congruence and similarity using physical models, transparencies, or geometry software
description: Students use informal arguments to establish and apply angle facts: the interior angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ$; an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles; and the angle pairs formed when a transversal cuts parallel lines (corresponding, alternate interior, alternate exterior, and co-interior/same-side interior angles). They then use the angle-angle (AA) criterion to argue that two triangles are similar and to find unknown angle measures.
subSkills: Apply the triangle angle-sum theorem to find a missing interior angle ($180^\circ$ total)
Apply the exterior-angle theorem (exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles)
Identify and use congruent angle pairs formed by parallel lines cut by a transversal (corresponding, alternate interior, alternate exterior)
Use supplementary co-interior (same-side interior) angles formed by parallel lines
Give an informal argument for why the angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ$ using parallel-line angle relationships
Apply the angle-angle (AA) criterion to determine whether two triangles are similar
Solve algebraic equations that arise from angle relationships to find a variable

problemArchetypes.name: Triangle angle sum (find the missing angle)
problemArchetypes.example: Two angles of a triangle measure $47^\circ$ and $68^\circ$. Find the third angle. Answer: $180^\circ - 47^\circ - 68^\circ = 65^\circ$.

problemArchetypes.name: Exterior angle theorem
problemArchetypes.example: In a triangle, the two remote interior angles measure $52^\circ$ and $71^\circ$. Find the exterior angle adjacent to the third vertex. Answer: $52^\circ + 71^\circ = 123^\circ$.

problemArchetypes.name: Parallel lines cut by a transversal (name and find an angle)
problemArchetypes.example: Lines $\ell$ and $m$ are parallel and cut by a transversal. One angle measures $113^\circ$. Find the measure of its alternate interior angle and of its co-interior (same-side interior) angle. Answers: $113^\circ$ (alternate interior, congruent) and $67^\circ$ (co-interior, supplementary).

problemArchetypes.name: Informal argument for the $180^\circ$ angle sum
problemArchetypes.example: Draw a line through one vertex of a triangle parallel to the opposite side. The two base angles equal the alternate interior angles along that line, which together with the top angle form a straight angle, so the three angles sum to $180^\circ$.

problemArchetypes.name: AA similarity criterion
problemArchetypes.example: Triangle $ABC$ has angles $40^\circ$ and $75^\circ$; triangle $DEF$ has angles $75^\circ$ and $65^\circ$. Are they similar? Both have angles $40^\circ, 75^\circ, 65^\circ$ (the third angles are $65^\circ$ and $40^\circ$), so by AA the triangles are similar.

problemArchetypes.name: Algebraic angle relationship
problemArchetypes.example: Corresponding angles formed by parallel lines are $(3x + 10)^\circ$ and $(5x - 24)^\circ$. Find $x$. Since corresponding angles are congruent, $3x + 10 = 5x - 24$, so $x = 17$.

problemArchetypes.name: Multi-step combined reasoning
problemArchetypes.example: A transversal crosses two parallel lines; an alternate interior angle is $58^\circ$ and forms one angle of a triangle whose second angle is $74^\circ$. Find the third angle of the triangle. Answer: $180^\circ - 58^\circ - 74^\circ = 48^\circ$.

Easy.description: Single-step application of one fact. The student substitutes given numeric angle measures into a single relationship (angle sum, one transversal pair, or one exterior angle) with no algebra.
constraints: Exactly one angle fact is needed
All given measures are whole-number degrees; the answer is a single subtraction or addition
No variables; named angle relationships are stated or obvious from the figure description
AA items at this level ask only whether two pairs of stated equal angles make triangles similar

Medium.description: Two-step reasoning or a one-variable equation. The student combines two facts (e.g., a transversal angle feeding a triangle angle sum) or sets up and solves a linear equation from congruent or supplementary angle expressions.
constraints: Requires either chaining two angle facts or solving a single linear equation in $x$
Angle expressions may be linear in $x$ (congruent pairs set equal, supplementary pairs summed to $180^\circ$)
May require correctly naming the angle pair (alternate interior vs. co-interior) before computing
AA items require finding the third angle of each triangle to confirm or reject similarity

Hard.description: Multi-step proofs or chains: combine parallel-line relationships, exterior-angle theorem, and AA similarity, or solve a system requiring multiple equations and substitution, and justify the reasoning.
constraints: Three or more linked steps, or an equation requiring distribution and combining like terms
May ask for an informal justification (which angle relationship and why) in addition to a value
May combine similarity (AA) with proportional side reasoning or with the exterior-angle theorem
Distractors must reflect plausible mis-identification of angle pairs or a sign error in the equation

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks the interior angles of a triangle sum to $360^\circ$ instead of $180^\circ$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For angles $47^\circ$ and $68^\circ$ gives $360^\circ - 47^\circ - 68^\circ = 245^\circ$ instead of $65^\circ$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats co-interior (same-side interior) angles as congruent instead of supplementary
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports the same-side interior angle of a $113^\circ$ angle as $113^\circ$ instead of $67^\circ$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats alternate interior angles as supplementary instead of congruent
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports the alternate interior angle of a $113^\circ$ angle as $67^\circ$ instead of $113^\circ$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student sets the exterior angle equal to one remote interior angle, or adds the adjacent interior angle instead of the two remote ones
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For remote interiors $52^\circ$ and $71^\circ$ gives $71^\circ$ (just one remote angle) instead of $123^\circ$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student adds the angle expressions of a congruent pair instead of setting them equal (or sets a supplementary pair equal instead of summing to $180^\circ$)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For congruent corresponding angles $(3x+10)^\circ$ and $(5x-24)^\circ$ writes $3x+10+5x-24 = 180$ giving $x = \frac{194}{8}$ instead of solving $3x+10 = 5x-24$ for $x = 17$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student believes two triangles are similar only if all three angles are explicitly given or if side lengths are equal, not recognizing AA is sufficient
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Declares triangles with two pairs of equal angles 'not enough information' instead of 'similar by AA'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses corresponding angles with vertical or linear-pair angles and uses the wrong relationship
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls a corresponding pair 'supplementary' and subtracts from $180^\circ$ instead of recognizing them as congruent
